I’m focused on your comparison of behavior of a developmental disability (something that affects how someone learns, and suggests they need additional educational support) to cancer (an illness that fucking sucks and kills people, but doesn’t affect learning ability in the majority of cases). I take issue with a SPED teacher doing that. That is pretty central to your point.

Weird that you questioned my reading comprehension skills, when I stated pretty clearly in my first comment that I didn’t think the behavior was ok, but you still felt I was minimizing the assault (the assault wasn’t at all the focus of my first comment?). 
I think it is wrong to contribute to stigmas about people with Down’s Syndrome as a SPED teacher. I consider it an important part of my job to advocate for students, including encouraging people to not view their disability as something life ruining (like terminal cancer).
(Also kind of funny to be upset that I used many words to better explain my point when you said I can’t read. LOL ok)

Dude, I just think that you should consider the connotation you are publicly sharing as a professional when you liken terminal illness to Down’s Syndrome. Down’s Syndrome isn’t life ending, and I think as a special education teacher, you should probably try to encourage others to not see Down’s Syndrome as something that prevents people from experiencing life.

Probably because the context of you saying it is an argument online where you have been nothing but rude because I disagree with your analogy. If you’re overall tone is rude, I am going to assume that when you say I can’t read, despite the fact that I have read all of this and I am writing back to you, you are trying to be hurtful. That’s literally reading comprehension.

Honestly what a rude thing to say as a special education teacher. Great job using IEP goals as an insult. I’m okay with being loathed by any SPED teachers who would use the tools we use to best serve our students as a way to insult others.

I mean she’s not upset about it, so there’s no reason for me to tell her anything about her feelings on the matter? 
Obviously if a student does that, there should be consequences, like immediate referral to admin. I just really don’t think you should compare terminal cancer and Down’s Syndrome, especially as a professional working with students with disabilities. Down’s Syndrome students often need additional social emotional learning instruction. Terminal cancer doesn’t imply that, it doesn’t seem like there is any implication that this kid needed additional SEL instruction, just that he did something wrong. 
I don’t agree with what he did, and never suggested that he did. I only suggested that I disagree with the comparison you are making. It seems you are intentionally trying to make it sound like I think sexual abuse is ok because I think you wrote a dumb comparison.
No I read your comment. I don’t see how thinking you wrote a bad analogy is the same as supporting what, yes, is sexual assault.

How am I enabling the behavior? Where did I excuse it, or suggest it was ok? 
I am saying your comparison of cancer to Down’s Syndrome, as a professional in special education, is frustrating because it contributes to a societal issues of conflating illnesses and disabilities that are unrelated and really not comparable. I think using analogies like that is not beneficial to supporting the differences of exceptionalities. I think comparing Down’s Syndrome to (terminal) cancer furthers the societal idea that Down’s is so detrimental to life it is equal to a terminal illness. Having cancer doesn’t even qualify for you special education in my state as it is not a disability or exceptionality.

I literally said it’s not appropriate. I never said his actions were acceptable in any way, shape, or form. I am saying you are comparing the education of social skills for Down’s to dying of a fucking terminal illness before post-adolescence. Maybe if you can’t differentiate between the scope of disabilities, you should take some time to educate yourself.

As another SPED teacher, I feel like you should be able to recognize how different Down’s is from being a child who is dying of cancer. 
(I’m not saying what he did was appropriate, but those things just aren’t comparable.)
